calls.title: Custom LLM Experiment Overview
calls.text: {"summary": "This experiment involved training a tiny word-level language model, Karpathy's nanoGPT, on two different corpora. The experiments compared training on a starter corpus alone versus a starter corpus augmented with custom teaching files.", "details": [{"text": "The custom LLM experiment uses a tiny word-level language model: Karpathy's nanoGPT, which has 2 blocks, 4 heads, 64-number embeddings, and 48-token context, and is trained from scratch on CPU.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "Two experiments were run with identical settings: one using the supplied starter corpus, and another using the starter corpus plus the starter corpus plus my own teaching files for grammar, opposites, and spatial relations.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "The model continues short sentences and is not a chatbot.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "Experiment 1 used the starter corpus, while Experiment 2 used the starter corpus plus three plain-text files: grammar_tense_and_agreement.txt, opposites_in_context.txt, and spatial_relations.txt.", "section": "S2"}, {"text": "The training steps were set to 3,000, which is considered enough practice for a model this small to learn the sentence patterns.", "section": "S3"}, {"text": "The learning rate was set to 0.001, which is large enough to make progress within 3,000 steps and small enough to avoid overshooting.", "section": "S3"}, {"text": "The vocabulary for Experiment 1 was 136, while for Experiment 2 it was 481.", "section": "S4"}, {"text": "The only fixed settings across both experiments included the seed 42, model size, batch size, steps, learning rate, the 48-case eval suite, and the eval generation settings.", "section": "S4"}]}

calls.title: Evidence and Loss Analysis
calls.text: {"summary": "Evidence and Loss Analysis involves examining samples and loss metrics from a Custom LLM Experiment. This analysis covers how text is tokenized, embedded, and how parameters are updated during training.", "details": [{"text": "Samples are recorded for experiments, with Experiment 1 and Experiment 2 having different sample sets.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "Step-0 samples were described as word soup, while by step 1,500, they wrote full sentences.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "Loss values are measured for fixed panels consisting of 20 training and 20 validation passages.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "Step-0 loss for Experiment 1 was about ln(vocabulary size): ln 136 ≈ 4.91, and for Experiment 2 was ln 481 ≈ 6.18.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "Tokenization converts text into tokens, which are then mapped to IDs, such as 'customer' being ID 28.", "section": "S2"}, {"text": "The embedding is a row of 64 numbers representing a word, and training adjusts these so similar words have similar numbers.", "section": "S2"}, {"text": "Next-token probabilities show the model's chances for the next word, and after training, verbs like 'reviewed' have a higher probability.", "section": "S2"}, {"text": "The first parameter update involves the gradient, which indicates the direction to nudge a number to reduce error.", "section": "S2"}]}

calls.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation Overview
calls.text: {"summary": "Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a technique that allows large language models (LLMs) to retrieve and incorporate new information from external data sources. This process supplements the LLM's pre-existing training data, enabling them to use domain-specific or updated information. RAG improves LLM performance by blending the LLM process with information retrieval to help LLMs stick to facts and reduce AI hallucinations.", "details": [{"text": "Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a technique that enables large language models (LLMs) to retrieve and incorporate new information from external data sources.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "RAG improves LLMs by incorporating information retrieval before generating responses.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "RAG pulls relevant text from databases, uploaded documents, or web sources.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "This method helps reduce AI hallucinations, which have caused chatbots to describe policies that don't exist, or recommend nonexistent legal cases to lawyers that are looking for citations to support their arguments.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "RAG also reduces the need to retrain LLMs with new data, saving on computational and financial costs.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "Beyond efficiency gains, RAG also allows LLMs to include sources in their responses, so users can verify the cited sources.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "The term retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) was introduced in a 2020 paper that described combining a parametric language model with a non-parametric external memory accessed through retrieval at inference time.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "Typically, the data to be referenced is converted into LLM embeddings, numerical representations in the form of a large vector space.", "section": "S4"}, {"text": "Given a user query, a document retriever is first called to select the most relevant documents that will be used to augment the query.", "section": "S4"}, {"text": "The model feeds this relevant retrieved information into the LLM via prompt engineering of the user's original query.", "section": "S4"}, {"text": "Finally, the LLM can generate output based on both the query and the retrieved documents.", "section": "S4"}, {"text": "RAG is used in applications where generated responses need to be grounded in external or frequently updated information.", "section": "S5"}]}

calls.title: Transformer Architecture
calls.text: {"summary": "The Transformer Architecture has primary components including tokenizers, an embedding layer, transformer layers, and an un-embedding layer. It operates by mapping text to numerical sequences, processing these sequences through layers that alternate between attention and feedforward mechanisms, and then converting the final representation back to a probability distribution over tokens.", "details": [{"text": "All transformers have the same primary components: Tokenizers, which convert text into tokens, Embedding layer, which converts tokens and positions of the tokens into vector representations, Transformer layers, which carry out repeated transformations on the vector representations, extracting more and more linguistic information, Un-embedding layer, which converts the final vector representations back to a probability distribution over the tokens.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "The input text is treated by a preprocessor, which performs both textual transformations and splits the text into coarse-grained segments called pretokens. The latter is referred to as pretokenization.", "section": "S2"}, {"text": "Each pretoken is segmented further into tokens by a tokenizer that expects to only see pretokens output by its preprocessor. Each token it produces is a string of one or more characters belonging to a finite set of strings called the vocabulary $V$.", "section": "S2"}, {"text": "Each integer token identifier is converted into an embedding vector via a lookup table. Equivalently stated, it multiplies a one-hot representation of the token identifier by an embedding matrix $M$.", "section": "S3"}, {"text": "The token embedding vectors are added to their respective positional encoding vectors (see below), producing the sequence of input vectors.", "section": "S3"}, {"text": "The dimension of an embedding vector is called hidden size or embedding size and written as $d_{\text{emb}}$. This size is written as $d_{\text{model}}$.", "section": "S3"}, {"text": "An un-embedding layer is a linear-softmax layer: $\text{UnEmbed} (x)=\text{softmax} (xW+b)$ The matrix has shape $(d_{\text{emb}},|V|)$.", "section": "S4"}, {"text": "A positional encoding is a fixed-size vector representation of the relative positions of tokens within a sequence: it provides the transformer model with information about where the words are in the input sequence.", "section": "S5"}, {"text": "The feedforward network (FFN) modules in a transformer are 2-layered multilayer perceptrons: $\text{FFN} (x)=\\phi (xW^{(1)}+b^{(1)})W^{(2)}+b^{(2)}$ where $W^{(1)}$ $W^{(2)}$ $b^{(1)}$ $b^{(2)}$ $\\phi$.", "section": "S7"}]}

calls.title: Transformer Training Methods
calls.text: {"summary": "Transformer training methods cover techniques for stabilizing training, regularization, pretraining and fine-tuning, knowledge distillation, and various language modeling tasks. These methods address issues like convergence, overfitting, and task-specific adaptation.", "details": [{"text": "The original paper recommended using learning rate warmup, where the learning rate linearly scales up from 0 to a maximal value for the first part of training before decaying.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "Using layer normalization before multihead attention and feedforward layers stabilizes training, which is the 'pre-LN Transformer' and is more commonly used compared to the original 'post-LN Transformer'.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "Dropout was applied to the output of each sublayer before its residual connection and normalization, as well as to the sums of token embeddings and positional encodings during the original transformer training to reduce overfitting.", "section": "S2"}, {"text": "The original paper also used label smoothing, which replaces a certain target distribution with one that assigns a small amount of probability to alternative tokens to improve generalization.", "section": "S2"}, {"text": "Transformers are typically first pretrained by self-supervised learning on a large generic dataset, followed by supervised fine-tuning on a small task-specific dataset.", "section": "S3"}, {"text": "Tasks for pretraining and fine-tuning commonly include language modeling, next-sentence prediction, question answering, reading comprehension, sentiment analysis, and paraphrasing.", "section": "S3"}, {"text": "Knowledge distillation is a method for training a smaller model, called a 'student', to reproduce the output behavior of a larger 'teacher' model using the teacher's output probability distribution, intermediate representations, or attention patterns.", "section": "S4"}, {"text": "Language modeling tasks are categorized into 'masked', 'autoregressive', and 'prefixLM' classes.", "section": "S5"}, {"text": "In a masked task, one or more tokens are masked out, and the model predicts a probability distribution for the masked-out tokens based on the context.", "section": "S5"}, {"text": "In an autoregressive task, the entire sequence is masked at first, and the model produces a probability distribution for the first token, which is then revealed to predict the second token, and so on.", "section": "S5"}, {"text": "In a prefixLM task, the sequence is divided into two parts, where the first part is presented as context, and the model predicts the first token of the second part, which is then revealed to predict the second token, and so on.", "section": "S5"}]}

calls.title: Transformer Efficient Implementations
calls.text: {"summary": "This topic covers various efficient implementations of the Transformer model, focusing on techniques to improve its performance and efficiency during inference and training. These implementations include methods for managing key and value vectors, optimizing batching, reducing model size through quantization, and developing faster attention mechanisms.", "details": [{"text": "The transformer model has been implemented in standard deep learning frameworks such as TensorFlow and PyTorch.", "section": "S1"}, {"text": "The KV caching method saves the computed key and value vectors at each attention block, so that they are not recomputed at each new token.", "section": "S2"}, {"text": "PagedAttention applies memory paging to KV caching.", "section": "S2"}, {"text": "If a transformer is used with a baked-in prompt, then the key and value vectors can be computed for the prompt, and saved on disk.", "section": "S2"}, {"text": "Continuous batching adds new requests to batch and removes completed requests between decoding iterations instead of waiting for every request in a batch to finish.", "section": "S3"}, {"text": "Transformer models are often quantized for inference, meaning that weights, activations, or both are represented with lower-precision numerical formats than the floating point formats used during training.", "section": "S4"}, {"text": "FlashAttention is an algorithm that implements the transformer attention mechanism efficiently on a GPU.", "section": "S5"}, {"text": "FlashAttention-2 offers enhancements in work partitioning and parallelism, enabling it to achieve up to 230 TFLOPs/s on A100 GPUs (FP16/BF16), a 2x speed increase over the original FlashAttention.", "section": "S5"}, {"text": "Multi-Query Attention changes the Multihead Attention mechanism by having just one $W^{K},W^{V}$ instead of multiple, which increases inference speed.", "section": "S6"}, {"text": "Multihead Latent Attention (MLA) is a low-rank approximation to standard MHA, which minimizes the KV cache by only caching a low-dimensional KV vector.", "section": "S6"}, {"text": "Speculative decoding is a method to accelerate token decoding by quickly computing future tokens and then verifying them.", "section": "S7"}, {"text": "Long Range Arena (2020) is a standard benchmark for comparing the behavior of transformer architectures over long inputs.", "section": "S8"}, {"text": "Reformer (2020) reduces the computational load from $O(N^{2})$ to $O(N\text{ln } N)$ by using sparse attention, and BigBird (2020) uses random small-world networks which grows as $O(N)$.", "section": "S9"}]}
